tools.name: search_guidelines
tools.description:
Look a rule up in the UMR guidelines (umr4nlp/umr-guidelines, guidelines.md).

keywords: terms to look for, e.g. "aspect", "modal strength", "have-rel-role-92", ":quant",
"reentrancy". Passages with more of the keywords come first, then those whose heading has
them, then those that mention them most.
max_results: how many passages to return (at most 10).

Returns {"sections": [{"heading": the passage's place in the guidelines ("Part 3. ... > Part
3-3-1. Aspect"), "text": the passage (a section, or a part of a long one)}], "found": how
many passages matched}.

tools.name: propbank_lookup
tools.description:
Look up a lemma and every alternate of it in PropBank (at most 20 per call).

language is "en" or "zh". Returns Markdown: per lemma, every roleset with its roles and all
its examples (the sentence, then each argument; traces such as *T*-1 are PropBank's own),
or "not in PropBank". Lemmas over the limit are not looked up: the last line names them
(call again with them). There is no PropBank for another language (Uzbek): nothing.

tools.name: search_annotations
tools.description:
Find how a case is annotated: gold UMR annotations of whole sentences.

language: "zh" (Chinese) or "en" (English).
keywords: words or pieces to look for, matched anywhere in a sentence or its annotation:
words of the text (e.g. "发生", "wanted to"), concepts ("have-org-role-91", "identity-91"),
roles (":ARG1-of", ":manner"), attribute values (":aspect state"). Sentences with more of the
keywords come first.
max_results: how many gold sentences to return (at most 10).

Returns {"gold": [{"doc", "sentence_number", "sentence", "annotation"}], where annotation is
the sentence's whole annotation (words, sentence-level graph, alignment, document-level
annotation); "found": how many gold sentences matched in all}.

content.content:
## 称呼

### 称呼-01

- ARG0: agent
- ARG1: entity arg0 calls
- ARG2: name arg1 is called

Example 1: 他 用 「 语言流 」 称呼 自己 的 语法
- ARG0: 他
- ARG1: 自己 的 语法
- ARG2: 用 「 语言流 」
- rel: 称呼

Example 2: 一时 之间 很多 朋友 都 不 称呼 我 的 名字 ， 而 叫 我 「 女 状元 的 爸爸 」
- ARG0: 很多 朋友
- ARG2: 我 的 名字
- ARGM-ADV: 不
- ARGM-ADV: 都
- ARGM-TMP: 一时 之间
- rel: 称呼

Example 3: *OP* 而 *pro* 吃 食 *T*-3 的 便 是 *OP* *T*-2 用 台语 称呼 —— 『 菜头糕 』 的 萝卜糕
- ARG1: *T*-2
- ARG2: —— 『 菜头糕 』
- ARGM-MNR: 用 台语
- rel: 称呼

Example 4: 反正 *OP* *T*-1 买 *pro* 的 人 也 都 不 问 *pro* *pro* 如何 称呼
- ARG1: *pro*
- ARGM-ADV: 如何
- rel: 称呼

## 称为

### 称为-01

- ARG0: name giver
- ARG1: name receiver
- ARG2: name

Example 1: 如果 传说 中 的 “ 西天 ” 是 个 “ 极乐世界 ” 的话 ， 那么 文部 草原 应当 称为 *OP* 当代 藏族 牧民 *T*-1 过上 社会主义 新 生活 的 “ 乐园 ”
- ARG1: 文部 草原
- ARG2: *OP* 当代 藏族 牧民 *T*-1 过上 社会主义 新 生活 的 “ 乐园 ”
- ARGM-CND: 如果 传说 中 的 “ 西天 ” 是 个 “ 极乐世界 ” 的话
- rel: 称为

Example 2: 防城港 、 钦州 、 北海 和 湛江 ， 被 人们 称为 西南 出海 大 通道 的 “ 龙头 ”
- ARG0: 人们
- ARG1: 防城港 、 钦州 、 北海 和 湛江
- ARG2: 西南 出海 大 通道 的 “ 龙头 ”
- rel: 称为

## 处理

### 处理-01

- ARG0: punisher
- ARG1: party punished

Example 1: 索珠乡 丁拉村 村支书 与 村委 主任 私 分 公款 的 情况 ， 在 财务 帐目 公开 时 被 *OP* 群众 发现 *T*-2 后 ， *pro* 及时 挽回 了 损失 ， 依法 处理 了 当事人 ， 推选 *OP* *T*-1 更为 合适 的 村委 主任 人选 。
- ARG0: *pro*
- ARG1: 当事人
- ARGM-TMP: 索珠乡 丁拉村 村支书 与 村委 主任 私 分 公款 的 情况 ， 在 财务 帐目 公开 时 被 *OP* 群众 发现 *T*-2 后
- ARGM-MNR: 依法
- rel: 处理

Example 2: 对 直接 责任人 和 主管 领导人 ， 不论 工作 是否 变动 ， *pro* 都 要 追究 责任 并 严肃 处理 。
- ARG0: *pro*
- ARG1: 对 直接 责任人 和 主管 领导人
- ARGM-CND: 不论 工作 是否 变动
- ARGM-ADV: 都
- ARGM-ADV: 严肃
- rel: 处理

### 处理-02

- ARG0: agent
- ARG1: theme

Example 1: 外交部 驻港 特派员 公署 致力 *PRO* 协助 特区 政府 *PRO* 处理 经 授权 的 对 外 事务
- ARG0: *PRO*
- ARG1: 经 授权 的 对 外 事务
- rel: 处理

Example 2: 举凡 *OP* *T*-1 涉及 世界 和平 与 安全 的 重大 事件 ， 只有 安理会 才 有 权 决定 *PRO* 如何 处理
- ARG0: *PRO*
- ARGM-ADV: 如何
- rel: 处理

### 处理-03

- ARG0: agent
- ARG1: theme
- ARG2: thing arg0 processes arg1 into being

Example 1: 只要 「 包装 」 好 一点 ， *pro* 处理 成 流行 趋势 、 理财 资讯 ， 不 要 太 像 广告 ， 一般 民众 大概 看 不 出来 新闻 後面 的 商业 利益
- ARG1: *pro*
- ARG2: 流行 趋势 、 理财 资讯
- rel: 处理

## 污染

### 污染-01

- ARG0: cause,agent
- ARG1: theme

Example 1: 这 种 方法 不 会 污染 环境 。
- ARG0: 这 种 方法
- rel: 污染

Example 2: 这 个 *OP* *T*-2 严重 污染 的 第三 大 淡水湖
- ARGM-ADV: 严重
- rel: 污染

{"sections": [{"heading": "Uniform Meaning Representation (UMR) 0.9 Specification > Part 4. Document-Level Representation > Part 4-2. Temporal Dependency > Part 4-2-1. Nodes in the temporal dependency", "text": "#### Part 4-2-1. Nodes in the temporal dependency There are three types of nodes in the temporal dependency structure: pre-defined metanodes, time expressions, and events. Pre-defined metanodes and time expressions make up the top levels of the dependency structure, called the temporal superstructure. `:depends-on` is the relation that is used to link all nodes in the temporal superstructure. [Back to Table of Contents](#toc)"}, {"heading": "Uniform Meaning Representation (UMR) 0.9 Specification > Part 4. Document-Level Representation > Part 4-2. Temporal Dependency > Part 4-2-2-1. Choosing the right temporal relation > Part 4-2-2-3. Causally-related events", "text": "##### Part 4-2-2-3. Causally-related events Causal relations between events are always annotated as `:after` relations. This means that in examples such as *the crops grew well because it rained enough*, `(rain :after grow)` is annotated even though the causing event (raining) and the caused event (growing) partly overlap. If the causal relationship is explicitly predicated, it is identified as a separate event. It is then annotated as `:after` the causing event, and the caused event is annotated as following it. Therefore, *the opening of the food can prompted my cat to meow* is annotated as `(open :after prompt)` and `(prompt :after meow)`. [Back to Table of Contents](#toc)"}, {"heading": "Uniform Meaning Representation (UMR) 0.9 Specification > Part 4. Document-Level Representation > Part 4-3. Modal Dependency > Part 4-3-1. Stage 0 > Part 4-3-1-6. Modal dependency structure", "text": "##### Part 4-3-1-6. Modal dependency structure At Stage 0, there are some pieces of the modal dependency structure that are unspecified. The modal strength that a modal verb imparts on its complement is one of these pieces. As the modal annotation progresses, this information is added to the frame files for modal verbs. For example, the complements of English *want* have a `:modstr NeutAff` value; this will be indicated in the frame file as shown below. ``` Predicate: want.01 Roles: Arg0: wanter Arg1: thing wanted Arg2: beneficiary Arg3: in-exchange-for Arg4: from :modstr of complement: NeutAff ``` For the complements of modals, the `:modstr` values work largely the same way that they do for other events; however, they reflect the beliefs of the `:experiencer` participant of the modal event, who is often not the author. For example, in (1), Mary believes that the visit event may take place in the future (`NeutAff` strength), but the author disagrees. \[4-3-1-6 (1)\] Mary wants to visit France next month, but I don’t think that’s possible. The value associated with the modal event in its frame file corresponds to Mary’s beliefs, as the `:experiencer` of the wanting event. Some predicates impart full, positive (`FullAff`) strength on their complements, often called factive predicates (e.g., *manage to*).
